entries.title: Matthew 22:2
segments: A certain king. In this parable of the royal marriage feast (

) Jesus repeats the truths and warnings of the preceding one.  God is meant by 'a certain king;' the 'servants' are the apostles; the 'rest,' or the remnant, are the chief priests, scribes and Pharisees.

entries.title: Matthew 22:7
segments: Burned their city. Jerusalem is meant.

entries.title: Matthew 22:9
segments: The partings of the highways. The territory of the Gentiles.  Since the Jews, the bidden guests, would not come to the marriage feast, the servants were to invite as many as they could find both bad and good.

entries.title: Matthew 22:11
segments: A man who had not on a wedding-garment. A serious offence according to eastern etiquette, and in the parable one that could easily have been avoided, as the king had provided a wedding garment for each of his guests.  The meaning is plain.  The wedding-garment is a righteous life, which alone gives the right to appear at the wedding feast.  The guests were judged.  Those who had the garment were accepted; he who was without it was condemned.

entries.title: Matthew 22:14
segments: Many are called, but few chosen. Referring most probably to the Jews of Christ's time.  Few were chosen because few responded to the call.  See

entries.title: Matthew 22:15
segments: Took counsel. Our Lord's replies were so exasperating to his accusers that the latter were resolved at all hazards to exhaust their ingenuity before giving up the attempt to entrap him in his own words.

entries.title: Matthew 22:16
segments: The Herodians. Partisans of the royal family of Herod.  They naturally strove to please the Romans and were unfriendly to the Pharisees.  Nevertheless the latter called them to their aid as being especially serviceable in case Jesus should give an entangling answer to a political question.

entries.title: Matthew 22:21
segments: Render therefore unto Caesar the things, etc. An argument against the union of church and state.  Each has its own duties and these are to be kept apart.  The Jews were commanded to obey Caesar in political matters, but to worship God in their religion.  In the latter respect Jesus defied Caesar, as in the former he upheld his authority.

entries.title: Matthew 22:22
segments: Marveled, and left him. The reply was altogether above and beyond their petty religious and political notions.  It showed how a universal religion could be made possible by separating it from any narrow national restrictions.

entries.title: Matthew 22:29
segments: Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures. The Sadducees, disbelieving in the resurrection, naturally sought to make light of it.  They were mistaken in supposing that if persons rose from the dead they would meet with conditions similar to those of the earthly life.

entries.title: Matthew 22:30
segments: As angels. This was a rebuke to the Sadducees in their denial of the existence of angels (
).  See

entries.title: Matthew 22:31
segments: Spoken unto you by God. That is, in the book of Exodus, a part of the Mosaic law in which they believed.

entries.title: Matthew 22:38
segments: The great and first commandment. It is probable that the Pharisee who asked this question did not do so in a hostile spirit.  At least it does not appear so from
.  Most likely it was intended as a fair test.  The reply of Jesus in
shows that he was pleased with his questioner.

entries.title: Matthew 22:39
segments: Love they neighbor as thyself. Not as a man ordinarily does love himself, that is, selfishly, but as he should love himself.

entries.title: Matthew 22:42
segments: The Christ. The Messiah.

entries.title: Matthew 22:44
segments:
Lord. God or Jehovah.
 

 
My Lord. The Lord of David, the Messiah that was to come.

entries.title: Matthew 22:45
segments: How is he his son? The reply of the Pharisees, acknowledging that the Christ, or Messiah, was the Son of David, was only partly acceptable to Jesus.  The psalm quoted by him in

implies that the Christ is also Lord of David and that he has a right to sit at the right hand of God.  Thus did Jesus prove to the Pharisees the divine authority of the Christ as Messiah from a psalm, which they fully accepted as Messianic.
